Name: Unsupported operating system version (no security updates since 2023)
Synopsis: The Linux distribution release on this host has reached end of support. The vendor no longer publishes security updates, so any new weakness found in it will never be fixed.
Solution: Retire the host, or move its inventory application to a supported, patched operating system. Until then, limit network access to the host and add it to the asset inventory with a named owner.

Name: FTP server version is unsupported and has publicly known vulnerabilities
Synopsis: The FTP service reports an old release that is no longer maintained. Publicly known vulnerabilities affect this release and will not be patched.
Solution: Turn off the FTP service if it is not needed. If file transfer is required, replace it with a supported secure file transfer service (for example SFTP) on a supported system.

Name: Windows monthly security updates missing (3+ months)
Synopsis: The credentialed check shows that three or more monthly Windows security update packages are not installed on these workstations.
Solution: Install all missing monthly updates. Find out why these devices stopped receiving updates, confirm they are enrolled in central update management, and retire any device that is no longer used.

Name: Database service reachable from the network with weak authentication
Synopsis: The database service accepts connections from other networks and allows accounts with weak or default-style credentials.
Solution: Bind the database to localhost or allow only the application host through a host firewall. Set strong unique passwords for every database account and remove unused accounts.

Name: Storage device firmware unsupported; web admin page exposed
Synopsis: This network storage device (NAS) runs firmware that the manufacturer no longer supports, and its web administration page is reachable from the server network.
Solution: Identify the owner and the data on the device. Move needed data to a supported, backed-up system and retire the device. If it must stay, restrict the admin page to IT management addresses only.

Name: Backup console uses default administrator account name
Synopsis: The backup console still uses the product's default administrator account name. Default names are widely known and make password-guessing easier.
Solution: Create named administrator accounts for each IT person, turn on MFA for the console if available, and disable or rename the default administrator account.

Name: TLS version 1.0 and 1.1 protocols enabled
Synopsis: The web server still accepts TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1. These old protocol versions have known design weaknesses and are no longer considered secure.
Solution: Turn off TLS 1.0 and 1.1 in the web server configuration and allow only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.

Name: SMB signing not required
Synopsis: The file server allows SMB connections without message signing. Without signing, a device on the network path could change or relay file-sharing traffic without being noticed.
Solution: Set the file server to require SMB signing (server signing = mandatory) and confirm that all clients support it.

Name: SSL/TLS certificate cannot be trusted (self-signed)
Synopsis: The certificate on this web interface is self-signed, so users cannot verify that they are connecting to the real server. Users learn to click through browser warnings.
Solution: Replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a trusted internal or public certificate authority.

Name: SSL/TLS certificate expired
Synopsis: The certificate on the backup console expired on 1 March 2025.
Solution: Issue and install a new certificate, and add certificate expiry dates to a renewal calendar or monitoring tool.

Name: SNMP agent accepts default community name
Synopsis: The printer's SNMP service answers to the manufacturer's default community name. Anyone on the network can read device and network details from it.
Solution: Change the community name to a long unique value, or better, switch to SNMPv3 with authentication. Turn SNMP off if the print vendor does not need it. Ask the print vendor to confirm the change.

Name: Web application login form sent over unencrypted HTTP
Synopsis: The inventory application login page sends usernames and passwords without encryption, so they can be read by anyone who can see the network traffic.
Solution: Serve the application only over HTTPS with a valid certificate and redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS.

Name: Remote access software detected (not on approved software list)
Synopsis: A vendor remote-support agent is installed and listening for connections. Remote access tools that IT did not approve can give outside parties a path into the network.
Solution: Confirm with the business owner whether the tool is needed. Remove it if not. If it is needed, approve it formally, record it in the software inventory, require MFA, and allow sessions only on request.

Name: SSH server supports weak key exchange algorithms
Synopsis: The SSH server still offers old key exchange algorithms that are no longer recommended.
Solution: Update the SSH server configuration to offer only modern key exchange algorithms. Moving the host to a supported operating system also fixes this.

Name: SSH server supports weak MAC algorithms
Synopsis: The SSH server still offers message authentication (MAC) algorithms that are considered weak.
Solution: Remove weak MAC algorithms from the SSH server configuration and allow only SHA-2 based algorithms.

Name: SSH server CBC mode ciphers enabled
Synopsis: The SSH server offers older CBC-mode encryption ciphers. Modern counter-mode (CTR) or GCM ciphers are preferred.
Solution: Remove CBC-mode ciphers from the SSH server configuration.

Name: FTP service allows cleartext authentication
Synopsis: The FTP service accepts usernames and passwords without encryption.
Solution: Turn off FTP (see plugin 900237) or require an encrypted file transfer method.

Name: ICMP timestamp request remote date disclosure
Synopsis: These hosts answer ICMP timestamp requests, which reveals their system clock. The risk is small, but it gives away information for free.
Solution: Block ICMP timestamp requests (type 13) and replies (type 14) at the host or network firewall.
